name: Economics of Uncertainty and Asymmetric Information
description:
This module examines decision problems involving uncertainty and asymmetric information using microeconomic methods.

Uncertainty arises when the outcome of a choice is subject to chance, i.e when a choice can lead to several mutually exclusive outcomes. For example, an employee with certain abilities may choose a certain level of effort which can result in a greater or lesser contribution to the firm's profits, depending on some random variables.

Asymmetric information exists when the parties to a transaction do not have the same level of information about relevant circumstances. For example, the owner of a firm may be unable to directly observe the ability and/or effort of an employee, nor can she infer them based on the employee's contribution to the firm's profit if that contribution is subject to chance.

The course introduces expected utility theory, the standard theory of rational decision-making under uncertainty. It examines risk sharing, both normatively and positively, analyzes the problems of moral hazard and adverse selection and studies contracts involving signaling and screening.

The concepts and methods covered in the course will be applied to specific problems and particular markets. Special emphasis will be placed on insurance markets and the principal-agent problem in firms.
